newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy mini-budget to snip not slash deficit.
newsitem.headline: Italy mini-budget to snip not slash deficit.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi will be hard pushed to make significant structural reforms in a mini-budget he intends to launch soon as part of his drive to make Italy a founding member of a European single currency.

Instead, economists say additional measures to rein in the country's excessive budget deficit will involve small snips in state spending which are unlikely to include any attempt at reforming the nation's pensions system.

"It will be difficult to come up with something structural. It's likely to be a blended combination of higher revenues and lower spending and then they'll leave bigger structural things to the 1998 budget," said Bruno Rovelli at BankAmerica here.

Prodi announced earlier on Wednesday he had a framework for extra 1997 measures to trim the budget deficit and enable Italy to meet criteria this year for joining European economic and monetary union (EMU) at its projected 1999 start.
The size of the package is not yet known nor is it likely to be decided definitively until the government has seen official state accounts which are due in March.
But analysts say for now they are expecting 10 to 20 trillion lire ($5.9-11.9 billion) in deficit-cutting measures, with several opting for a narrower range of 13 to 15 trillion.
Andrea Marchetti, analyst at Credito Italiano here, said if the government went for a larger package of 20 to 25 trillion, then it would need to include welfare and health system reforms.
"But in the case of a 10 to 13 trillion lire package, Prodi will try to avoid welfare reform in 1997," he said.

One problem is that few structural measures, like welfare and health system reforms, will take effect quickly enough to affect state accounts in 1997, the year on which the performance of those states wishing to join EMU will be judged.

Economists say without a mini-budget Italy will have a deficit of 70 to 72 trillion lire and a deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) ratio of 3.5 to 3.8 percent, above the 3.0 percent required for EMU.
With additional measures, the deficit should shrink maybe as far as 63-64 trillion lire or just above the 3.0 percent ratio.
Pressure is on Prodi from all directions to steer clear of tax hikes after the government turned the fiscal screw with an unpopular one-off "Eurotax" levy at the end of last year.

Analysts say some options include possible welfare spending cuts, more efficiency in public administration, more cuts in payment transfers to local authorities and more advances on severance payments -- most of which were in the last package.
In addition, Chiara Manenti, economist at Caboto here, said some two to three trillion could be raised through a one-off tax on pension contributions and maybe wages.
Rovelli also did not rule out small levies but doubted there would be any major tax rises.
All this is unlikely to satisfy financial markets baying for a second round of tougher reforms to Italy's generous pension system to follow up changes worked out in 1995.

Analysts argue as far as 1997 is concerned, there is no time for the debate needed with the hard-left Communist Refoundation party, whose support ensures a majority for Prodi in the lower house but which is adamantly against touching pensions.
Even if there were time, effects of pension reforms would barely kick in quickly enough to affect this year's accounts.

Instead, the long-sought pensions debate is expected to start this year but it remains to be seen whether the government will then wait for the 1998 appointment agreed with trade unions to take action on reviewing the 1995 reforms.
